analysis.one_liner: Fees on large data centers and cryptomining for fossil-fuel electricity, funding consumer rebates and clean power.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2025 with one cosponsor, the bill has sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge large data centers and cryptocurrency mining operations for the fossil-fuel emissions behind their electricity, with a fee that rises each year and a requirement to reach zero-emissions power by 2035. Utilities could not pass the fee on to regular customers. Most of the money collected would go back to lowering household electricity bills and to building zero-carbon power and long-duration battery storage.
analysis.who_benefits: Households facing rising electricity bills from data center and cryptomining demand — 25% of collected fees would fund grants to lower residential energy costs. Everyone breathing regional air gains from a grid that must decarbonize for these facilities, and 70% of the money would fund zero-carbon power plants and long-duration storage. Ordinary ratepayers are specifically protected: utilities are barred from recovering the fee by raising rates on any customer that is not a covered facility, with a penalty of twice the amount improperly recouped.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households facing data-center-driven power bill increases

how_it_helps.text: Fees apply only to electricity from emissions above a regional baseline that falls 11% of its original level each year from 2027 through 2034 and reaches zero in 2035, pushing large computing facilities onto clean power over time.

25% of collected fees are appropriated as grants to states, tribes, municipalities, and utilities for programs that lower residential electricity costs, such as direct rebates, specifically to offset cost increases caused by data center electricity consumption.
70% of collected fees fund zero-carbon electricity generation that runs at high capacity year-round and long-duration energy storage that can discharge for at least 10 hours.

Electric utilities may not recoup the fee by raising rates or fees on any customer that is not a covered facility, and must pay a fine of twice anything they improperly recoup — insulating ordinary ratepayers from the cost.

The EPA must publish, for every covered facility, its location, whether it is a data center or cryptomining operation, its owner, its fuel mix, and its emissions intensity — creating public transparency about where these facilities are and what powers them.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of data centers and cryptomining facilities above 100 kilowatts of installed computing power that run on electricity more emissions-intensive than their region's baseline — the fee starts at $20 per metric ton of excess emissions per kilowatt-hour and rises $10 each year plus inflation. Electric utilities serving those facilities are on the hook for the grid portion of the fee, though they may charge the covered facility itself. Hyperscale cloud and AI companies and Bitcoin miners with fossil-heavy power would bear the direct cost; the public could also see some pass-through in cloud, streaming, and AI service prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large data center and cryptomining operators

drawbacks.text: The fee schedule is steep and escalates from $20 per ton of excess emissions, rising $10 per year plus inflation, with the baseline reaching zero by 2035 — effectively a mandate that large computing facilities run on fully zero-carbon power, whose costs could be passed to consumers through cloud, streaming, and AI service prices.

Cryptocurrency mining is highly mobile — the bill's own findings note that the largest share of Bitcoin mining shifted to the United States by mid-2021 — so a US-only fee could push mining to countries with dirtier grids, raising global emissions even if US emissions fall.

The coverage threshold is low — any data center or mining operation with more than 100 kilowatts of installed computing power — which captures smaller server operations and imposes annual reporting on them, while their location, owner, and fuel mix become public even though consumption figures stay confidential.

The ban on utilities recovering the fee from non-data-center customers depends on EPA monitoring of rate data, which the bill itself acknowledges requires ongoing enforcement and could be difficult to verify in complex utility rate structures.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is unusually targeted: the industries whose electricity use is driving up regional demand and emissions pay the fee, 25% of the money flows back directly to household bills, and ordinary ratepayers are legally shielded from pass-through with a doubled-penalty backstop. The strongest honest objections are cost pass-through into digital services (the bill cannot stop a cloud or AI provider from raising subscription prices) and the possibility that mobile cryptomining simply relocates abroad rather than shutting down. Those are real limits, but they do not undo the consumer and grid benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and has sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote ever since.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on April 10, 2025, with Senator John Fetterman joining as its only cosponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction.
The complete action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — for the remainder of the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large data center and cryptomining operators are better off so far: without committee action, no fees, disclosure requirements, or clean-power mandates ever take effect, and energy-intensive computing can keep expanding on the existing grid.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data center and cryptomining operators, for now

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; the bill's only two attached lawmakers are both Senate Democrats, with 1 of 45 Senate Democrats cosponsoring, and no Republican is on the record either way.

industries.note: Proof-of-work mining is energy-intensive by design, and the bill's findings note that retired fossil plants are being brought back online to power it. Every kilowatt-hour above the regional baseline would carry a fee that escalates to a zero-emissions requirement by 2035.

industries.industry: Data center and cloud computing companies
industries.note: Fossil-powered facilities would pay escalating fees on grid and behind-the-meter electricity and face public disclosure of their locations, owners, and fuel mix. Facilities powered entirely by zero-carbon sources around the clock are exempt, so the bill costs the dirtiest operators most and hands clean operators an advantage.

Utilities would owe the fee on above-baseline power sold to covered facilities but are barred from recovering it from ordinary customers, with a doubled-penalty backstop. Some could also benefit as eligible recipients of the bill's clean-firm generation and storage grants.

industries.industry: Zero-carbon power and long-duration storage developers
industries.note: 70% of collected fees fund grants, rebates, and low-interest loans for zero-carbon generation running above 70% capacity factor and storage that discharges for at least 10 hours — a large, dedicated new revenue stream for clean firm power.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has one cosponsor and no committee action after months of in a Senate where Republicans hold 55 seats and control the Environment and Public Works agenda. Bills at this stage with no hearing or markup almost never reach the floor; unless support widens substantially, it will likely remain pending and die quietly when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
